text: Walk the East Eagle Trail up the valley for about 1.5 mi, then leave it and head right into the steep basin on Krag Peak's west side. The line climbs the loose, steep rib that divides two prominent drainages; stay on the crest of the rib rather than in the gullies either side. Expect sections of exposure with big loose blocks, and test every hold. The rib tops out on the west (northwest) summit. From there, traverse the crest to the slightly higher east summit, then continue along the ridge crest before descending the rubbly slopes toward Crater Lake. From the lake, pick up the Little Kettle Creek Trail and follow its many switchbacks back down to the East Eagle Trailhead.
runs: the loose steep rib that divides two prominent drainages

text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: park 1.1 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, where a dirt road intersects the paved road on the left (SE side), or continue to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.
runs: park 1.1 miles past the middle point ridge trailhead where a dirt road intersects the paved road on the left se side
megadike north park 1.1 miles past the middle point ridge trailhead where a dirt road intersects the paved road on the left se side or

text: Also published as 'A Slave to Liberty' (450m, Grade V, 5.13-). Climbs the first three pitches of Freedom or Death (5.10, 5.11, 5.11), then breaks right to join Thin Red Line just below its third-pitch anchor before launching into eight new pitches (four rated 5.12) up the East Face, with the crux 5.13 slab on pitch 8. Mikey Schaefer began equipping the line in 2015 and completed a one-day free ascent, leading every pitch, in early August 2016 with Shanjean Lee's support.
runs: 5.13 climbs the first three pitches of freedom or death 5.10 5.11 5.11 then

text: Climbs the first three pitches of Freedom or Death (5.10, 5.11, 5.11), then a right-leaning overlap (P4, 5.12-) into a traverse with layback flakes and a mantle (P5, 5.12-), an arete with a big hand-rail traverse (P6, 5.12), a 165 ft 'mega slab' pitch with 14 bolts and 4 crux moves (P7, 5.12+), and a razor-thin slab crux (P8, 5.13-) before easing off through P9-P11 (5.10-5.10+).
runs: climbs the first three pitches of freedom or death 5.10 5.11 5.11 then

text: Walk back up the road toward the pass to a pond on its south side, and from the pond's east end follow the cairned climbers' path about a mile through forest to the East Face talus. Climb the first three pitches of Freedom or Death, step right onto Thin Red Line just below its third anchor, and follow this route's eight pitches; from the top, scramble to the summit roped.
runs: the first three pitches of freedom or death

text:
Same East Face approach as Freedom or Death and Thin Red Line: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the East Face talus.

This route was equipped largely rope-solo and first freed in August 2016 and originally documented under an earlier name. It climbs the first three pitches of Freedom or Death, then steps right onto Thin Red Line just below its third-pitch anchor before eight new pitches of its own.
runs: climbs the first three pitches of freedom or death

text: Abernathy Peak is the high point of Abernathy Ridge, between the Twisp River and Wolf Creek drainages in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. The more heavily traveled standard route climbs from Scatter Lake on the south side (class 2); the North Ridge described here is a quieter, more sustained class 2-3 alternative reached from Wolf Creek and Gardner Meadows to the north, climbing past an old mining camp at a small tarn and up a spur ridge onto the crest before scrambling to the summit.
runs: peak is the high point of abernathy ridge

text: This is the side every recorded ascent of the north ridge has come from. Maps show an old trail running west from Gardner Meadows toward a mine at a small tarn on the peak's northeast side, but there is very little evidence of it leaving the meadows and it is effectively abandoned: parties bushwhack along its rough line, picking up occasional cairns and cut logs, and the tread only firms up nearer the tarn. Expect the trail to peter out past the campsites and the going to become a matter of climbing over, around and under downed timber. Keep above the lake below the ridge rather than dropping to it. The north side can also be entered from the North Creek valley on the far side of the range, but that way is undescribed, so the marks below are written for this approach rather than that one.
runs: a mine at a small tarn on the

text: P1-P4 and most of P5 are the standard Let It Burn line, then two pitches (5.12- and 5.11-) lead into the West Face finish. P1 (5.8): ramp to a thin splitter crack, tree belay. P2 (5.10+): another short splitter, walk left to a second tree belay. P3 (5.12-): a few 5.10 cracks past a 5.11 slot where the old fixed pin has been removed, leaving a good cam placement; crux is two bolts moving left; belay at a two-bolt anchor. P4 (5.11a): hands and fingers crack to knobs and a double crack; belay at a fixed pin and bolt. P5 (5.11+): flare crack becoming a lieback; belay on 1" gear on a rightward bench. P6 (5.12-): a difficult flake/crack sequence; belay in the chimney right of a razor flake. P7 (5.11-): tips V-slot to a roof, then a corner. P8 (5.11+): hand crack to a roof. P9 (5.10): overhanging chimneys to a large ledge. P10 (5.6): easy 300 feet to the summit.
runs: and most of p5 are the standard let it burn
walk left to a second tree belay p3 5.12
double crack belay at a fixed pin and
belay on 1 gear on a rightward bench p6 5.12
right of a razor flake p7 5.11 tips v slot to a roof then
overhanging chimneys to a large ledge p10 5.6 easy 300 feet

text: Hands and fingers on knobs, fins and thin cracks, stepping right twice into new crack systems, to a double crack. Belay at a fixed pin and a bolt on a small ledge.
runs: knobs fins and thin cracks stepping right twice into new crack systems
double crack belay at a fixed pin and a bolt

text: New terrain. Traverse right, then climb a gently overhanging line of thin cracks and tips locks. The crux passes a wedged flake that flexes, so gear placements beside it are unreliable. Belay in a small alcove in the chimney just right of a razor-sharp flake. Grades for this pitch range from 5.11c to 5.12-.
runs: of thin cracks and tips locks the crux
in the chimney just right of a razor

text: New terrain. Awkward body positions up a tips crack in a V-shaped flare lead to a stance under a 4 ft roof where the corner switches from right-facing to left-facing. Good gear overhead protects a double hand-jam pull over the roof into thin hands, which fights up to a ledge. Grades given run from 5.11- to mid-5.11.
runs: where the corner switches from right facing to left facing

text: High clearance helpful late season; parking only on the right side of FR 7601 between Eightmile Lake and the trailhead, and the lot fills before dawn on summer weekends.
runs: on the right side of fr 7601 between eightmile lake and

text: A new route on the steep east face of South Peak featuring challenging crack and face climbing on white granite.
runs: new route on the steep east face of south

text: Start in the large corner in the middle of the east face and climb the splitter finger and hand cracks on the wall right of the corner, up out of the moat to a ledge on the right. Good-quality climbing; this is the best pitch of the route.
runs: up out of the moat to a ledge on the right

text: Finish via the standard North Face route by traversing Burgundy Ledge to its rappel line, or continue on rambling terrain (up to 5.7) directly to the summit.
runs: the standard north face route by traversing burgundy ledge

text: About 5-10 minutes below the col via loose rock/snow scramble to a clean splitter flake; P1 climbs the flake system to a roof pull and lieback on the left.
runs: flake system to a roof pull and lieback on the left

text: Eight pitches: a flake system to a roof pull and lieback, a right-trending finger crack, then the lichened, steep 5.10c finger crack that is the crux. Fourth-class ground trends left to a chimney, then a poor-rock corner and steep, thinly-protected bulges at 5.10 with the belay beyond the arete. The last pitch either rambles up to 5.7 past an old bolt to the skyline and the true summit, or traverses Burgundy Ledge into the standard North Face route — the descent is the North Face rappel line either way.
runs: flake system to a roof pull and lieback

text: Doubles of cams from 0.4 in to #3 with a few smaller cams and one #4-equivalent; full nut set.
runs: 3 with a few smaller cams and one 4

text: Rack doubles from 0.4-3 inches with a few smaller cams and one #4, plus a set of nuts.
runs: with a few smaller cams and one 4

text: A fun flake system to a roof pull and lieback on the left; the scramble concludes at a horn wrapped in fixed webbing.
runs: fun flake system to a roof pull and lieback on the left

text: A single rappel from the ledge system down to the ledge at the bottom of the third pitch.
runs: to the ledge at the bottom of the third pitch

text: Described as the recommended route: gain Asa Peak's Northeast Ridge, traverse to Agnes's south ridge, and climb short technical sections up to 5.6-5.8. From a high camp near Icy-Spruce Pass, parties make a rising traverse over snow, talus, and slabs to the south ridge crest south of Point 7760, then rope up for several pitches of Class 4-5 rock on or left of the crest. Where the crest gets too craggy, downclimb one pitch to a ledge system and traverse to a whaleback with views of the summit block. From the 7,480-ft south col, traverse a high snowpatch and ascend a broad Class 2-3 ramp just left of a snow-filled gully, dog-legging right to a headwall; a 5.8 chimney (the crux) and one more roped pitch lead to a final ~100-ft Class 2-3 scramble to the summit.
runs: several pitches of class 4 5 rock on or left of the crest

text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on the Minidike: park 1.5 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead on the left (SE) side of the road, just after crossing a bridge over the river. Cross the road, scramble down the bridge abutment, and follow a trail downstream on the NW side.
runs: park 1.5 miles past the middle point ridge trailhead on the left se side of the road just after crossing a bridge over the river

text: From the glacier directly below the northeast face, traverse (or first climb to near the col northwest of the peak) to reach the mixed rock and snow of the upper NE face. A large 45-degree snow gully, reached by a traverse onto the rock face, is a key feature; above it, the line moves south on pleasant, moderate rock (mostly class 3, occasional class 4), with snow patches often persisting until late summer.
runs: from the glacier directly below the northeast face
the mixed rock and snow of the upper ne face
a large 45 degree snow gully reached by a traverse onto the rock face

text: Beyond the notch, descend a steep dirt chute between snow and rock, then contour at roughly 5,800 ft above the moraine bowl. From there angle north through a series of steep gullies and ribs to the saddle. Route-finding, not difficulty, is what costs time on this section, and the red talus is loose throughout.
runs: a steep dirt chute between snow and rock then

text: Follow a faint climbers' path along the crest for about two hundred yards, then traverse right onto slabby red ledges near a rock rib. A cleft just left of the rib and more slabby ledges gain a flat step on top of it; a down-sloping bench then crosses to the mouth of a steep snow gully, where a tall snow fin splits the gully and you take a moat on either side or the hole through the fin itself. From the notch above, two pitches of the Great Chimney lead to the top — a 5.3 entry, then a smooth 5.4 face move over a large chockstone and a squeeze so tight that packs have to be pushed through ahead of the climber. Above the chimney a dirty slabby trough, a row of horns and gaps, and one dramatically exposed step-across finish the climb.
runs: to the mouth of a steep snow gully

text: Accounts disagree on the count. One party made three rappels on the way down; another made two from the top of the keyhole to reach the bottom. A third account describes five rappels, but that is one party’s descent on two 25 m ropes rather than a list of fixed stations — which is why its lengths (about 23 m / 75 ft) look so precise and why its count disagrees with the others. That party’s final rappel off the southeast rib jammed and they sacrificed a rope; the standard line threads the low keyhole beneath the chockstone for a cleaner pull.
runs: from the top of the keyhole to reach the bottom

text:
The 6,200-6,300 ft notch on Larrabee's northwest rib is the first gate, and the South Ambo Saddle at about 6,840 ft is the second. Those two are the whole navigation of this approach and both are cols — places where the ridge is low and you can stand on the crest with ground falling away on the far side. In cloud you are counting cols, not looking at the peak.

Between them is a red talus and moraine bowl. From the notch you drop slightly into it and then climb north out of it, up and across a series of steep gullies and ribs, to the saddle. Red rock underfoot after the first col is the confirmation you are in the right bowl.

Arrival at the saddle: it is on the ridge crest directly south of the summit. Standing there, the peak is north of you and Larrabee is behind you to the south. That bearing is the check — this is not a saddle you reach with the mountain to one side.

Where the climbing actually starts is 200 yards above the saddle, not at it. From the saddle, go up the ridge crest on a faint climbers' path for roughly 200 yards, then start traversing rightward on slabby red ledges. The rock scrambling begins where the angle steepens noticeably at a distinctive rock rib: the first real move is up a small Class 3.5 cleft closely left of that rib.

De Gaulle's Nose is the aiming mark on the far side of the red face, at about 7,300 ft. The rising traverse across the red slopes goes toward it and the crossing feels very exposed. Beyond it come two 60-metre gullies with a sand-covered ledge traverse between them, and a chimney at the top of the second reached by a very airy ledge. If your route has no red traverse and no pair of long gullies, it is not this one.

And the hard condition rule: do not attempt the Larrabee sidehill on wet grass or wet rock. Parties flag that as a genuine no-go rather than a discomfort.
runs: up and across a series of steep gullies and ribs

text: Hike east along the crest to a small col southwest of the North Ridge, then descend a 3rd-class gully down the north slope.
runs: hike east along the crest to a small col

text: Set of stoppers, doubles from BD #0.3 to #2, plus a single #3.

The route climbs cracks on the NW side of the buttress, starting on a steep slab with a thin vertical crack, with the crux on pitch 3.

text: The count is the test. Middle Finger Buttress is the biggest feature on the wall, and Ka'aba — where this route is — sits two buttresses to its left. So find the biggest one first, then count two left. Ka'aba itself is blocky and stepped, described as looking like stepping stones, which is quite unlike the clean sweep of Middle Finger. Be aware that the two buttresses between them are unnamed, so the count is the only handle you have — there is no known left-to-right inventory of this wall. Arrival is a large block at the base that you scramble onto for the first pitch, and getting onto it has a known seasonal trap. Approaching from the left side of the block runs into a large snow moat that stopped one party in early July. The right side goes, though it needs some care on friction moves crossing the top of the block to reach the wall. Walk-off, and there are two. The short one is a gully on the north side about a thousand feet east of Ka'aba, roughly thirty-five to forty degrees, giving a half-mile return to the lake — but it can hold firm snow through July. The longer one circles south around Amphitheater's western arm on sand and then meadows with a decent trail, rejoining the Boundary Trail and returning to the lake in about two miles and fifty minutes of easy walking.
runs: friction moves crossing the top of the block to

text: A crimpy start leads to a crystal pocket and a small overlap, then excellent friction slab. Carry one 0.2 cam; the crux can be aided at roughly 5.10. From the ledge atop this pitch, an easy corner out left avoids the last pitch.
runs: crimpy start leads to a crystal pocket and

text: From the Dosewallips Ranger Station (the road-walk/bike-in described separately covers reaching this point, since the Dosewallips River Road washout has closed vehicle access since 2002), pick up the Dosewallips River Trail and go about 1.4 miles to the signed junction with the West Fork Dosewallips Trail. Turn up the West Fork Trail and follow the river valley through old-growth forest roughly 8 miles to Honeymoon Meadows (3,527 ft) — this is the last reliable flat camping and dependable water before the climb, though the West Fork ford here (and a second crossing near Diamond Meadow lower down) can run thigh-deep and swift in early season or after rain, and the trail has substantial blowdown because NPS maintenance has lagged since the road closure. From Honeymoon Meadows continue up switchbacks about 1.2 more miles to Anderson Pass (4,464 ft), the Dosewallips/Quinault divide and junction with the Enchanted Valley trail — roughly 16 miles and the end of maintained tread. At the pass, leave the trail and follow a climbers' boot path north over talus and heather benches about a mile and 700+ ft of gain to the Anderson Glacier moraine (~5,200 ft), passing a small tarn; this is the customary high camp. From the moraine, ascend along the glacier margin/moraine crest toward Flypaper Pass (6,500 ft), the notch between Mount Anderson to the east and 7,033-ft Echo Rock to the west — historically a steep snow finger, now increasingly bare scree and, late season, exposed ice as the finger has receded, making an ice axe/crampons and careful footing important; this section is best done in spring or early summer before it melts out. Anderson's Thumb is the prominent sandstone pinnacle in this Flypaper Pass/Echo Rock vicinity (visible from the Anderson Glacier basin around 5,250 ft); below the pass, bear west under Echo Rock and scramble talus and ledges to its base. No water is reliably available above the Anderson Glacier moraine besides snowmelt, so fill up at camp.
runs: best done in spring or early summer before

text: 3 single-rope rappels, sometimes 4: one from the upper rock band to a ledge on the southeast face, then two or three down the gully just east of the top of the Northeast Couloir to the snow. Anchors are natural and may need rigging. Some parties instead make two rappels down slabs north of the east gully and traverse a wet ledge into it.
runs: gully just east of the top of the

text: From the summit, descend back to the upper rock band and make a single rappel to the ledge on the southeast face; you may need to rig a natural anchor, and one party used a slung tree there. Then head over to the top of the Northeast Couloir and find the gully just east of it: two or three single-rope rappels down that gully reach the snow slopes below. Anchors are natural and not reliably in place, so carry webbing and nuts to build them. Alternatively, some parties make two rappels down the slabs just north of the east gully, off slings around blocks and a small tree, then traverse a wet, snow-covered ledge into the gully. Either way, finish with a roughly 2,500 ft glissade down the Colchuck Glacier to the lake, then out via the Colchuck Lake trail. Another option drops via a different gully into Porcupine Creek Basin with a traverse around Colchuck Peak.
runs: from the summit descend back to the upper rock band
down the slabs just north of the east gully

text: This table follows the southeast-face ledge line. The other descent makes two rappels down slabs just north of the east gully and then traverses a wet ledge into it. Choose one line before you leave the summit.
runs: slabs just north of the east gully and

text: Natural, and not guaranteed to be in place — you may need to rig the anchor yourself, and one earlier party describes rappelling from a slung tree on the southeast-facing ledge. Carry webbing and nuts for this descent.
runs: a slung tree on the southeast facing ledge

text: From the summit, descend back to the upper rock band; the single rappel from there drops onto the ledge on the southeast face.
runs: from the summit descend back to the upper rock band

text: Natural / rigged; an older two-rope description used a stopper anchor part way up the southeast face.
runs: a stopper anchor part way up the southeast face

text: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of the highway near milepost 161, just west of Washington Pass, at about 5,200 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.
runs: a northwest forest pass is required to park

text: From Eldorado camp, traverse the Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col, pass through the col, and follow the north ridge along the McAllister Glacier to a break at about 7,900 ft, where climbers rappel 75 ft to the Klawatti Glacier. From there, 4th and easy 5th class climbing for about 150 ft gains the sub-summit; a further short pitch (roughly 50 ft of contrived low 5th class climbing on loose rock) on the summit tower reaches the true summit.
runs: through the col and follow the north ridge
4th and easy 5th class climbing for about 150

text: Rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier northeast at roughly 7,800 ft, continuing well past Eldorado's own summit and the Tepeh Towers to the col on Klawatti's flank. Pass through the col and follow Klawatti's north ridge along the upper reaches of the McAllister Glacier to the break in the ridge at about 7,900 ft.
runs: along the upper reaches of the mcallister glacier to

text: Leave the glacier where the traverse runs out below the peak and scramble a few hundred feet of 4th class, then trend and traverse left along a broken ridge to the sub-summit. A final short pitch of well-protected low 5th class swings right onto the northeast face to the true summit; the rock on the summit tower is loose enough to be worth belaying.
runs: a few hundred feet of 4th class then trend and traverse left

text: Pass through Klawatti col and follow Klawatti's north ridge along the upper McAllister Glacier to a break in the ridge at about 7,900 ft. Cross the moat and rappel 75 ft to the Klawatti Glacier from an old anchor. Getting back up on the return is a short belayed pitch graded 5.5–5.6 (stay left in the gully), so carry a small rack and retrievable cord.
runs: mcallister glacier to a break in the ridge at

text: Leave packs and crampons at the rock. One line climbs a few hundred feet of 4th class, traverses left on a broken ridge, and finishes with about 30 ft of low 5th around to the right on the northeast face, which can be soloed or simul-climbed. An easier class 3 line on the southeast ridge also reaches this sub-summit, where most parties stop.
runs: around to the right on the northeast face

text:
The base is a break in the ridge at about 7,900 ft that you rappel into, not walk through. That is the single most useful thing to know here: the correct notch takes about 75 ft of rope to get down onto the Klawatti Glacier, and on the way back it is roughly 75 ft of well-protected 5.5 to climb out. A gap you strolled through is Klawatti Col, one col short, at about 7,800 ft.

Get there by counting, not by sighting Austera. Cross the Inspiration to Klawatti Col; pass Klawatti Peak on your left through that col; follow the ridge along the upper McAllister Glacier about 0.4 mile to the second break. Austera is the high point of a whole arête of towers and picking it out from below is not a reliable way to navigate.

Above the glacier traverse the climbing is short and countable: a few hundred feet of 4th class gains a sub-summit, and a further short pitch — about 30 to 50 ft of low fifth, taken around to the right on the northeast face — reaches the true top.

The false summit is the real hazard on this peak, and it is the test that matters. Parties top out a few feet short of the true summit again and again. The true summit is reached only after crossing a narrow, often snowy ridge between two blocks and climbing a short chimney or a few feet of low fifth beyond it. If you got to where you are standing without a rope-worthy move and without crossing that ridge, you are on the false summit and the mountain is not finished with you.

The moat beside the rappel point is the thing most likely to change year to year; check it on the way in, because it has to work in the other direction at the end of the day.
runs: around to the right on the northeast face

text: The traverse ends at a small notch at the base of Klawatti's north ridge, and getting down from it onto the Klawatti Glacier is the crux of the whole traverse. Early in the season it downclimbs; as the moat opens through the summer it needs a rappel of roughly 75 ft, and the lowest notch can push into class 5 with class 4 ground to its southeast. Old rappel anchors turn up here — treat any in-place tat as suspect and carry cord to back it up or replace it. On the way back, some parties climb well-protected rock out of the glacier rather than rig a rappel.
runs: a small notch at the base of klawatti's north ridge

text: From the West Fork Methow River Trailhead (River Bend Campground, ~2,700 ft, at the end of Lost River Road/FR 5400), follow the West Fork Methow River Trail roughly 8 miles up-valley to its junction with the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT) at Brush Creek. Turn left (south/west) on the PCT and follow it about 1.5-2 miles, crossing Jet Creek, to Horse Heaven Camp (~4,350 ft) — the last reliable, easy water before the climb (treat before drinking; flows can drop significantly by late season). From camp, pick up the old, unsigned Azurite Pass (Mill Creek) trail, which departs the PCT roughly 120 yards east of the Jet Creek crossing at a small rock cairn — easy to miss, and parties note the tread is faint/braided enough that a GPS track is genuinely useful here. The path switchbacks up through slide-alder brush, firms up into a real trail around 5,000 ft, re-crosses Jet Creek at about 5,300 ft (a rock-hop ford, can run high with snowmelt in June/early July), then climbs through eroded, brushy benches before breaking out into open heather meadows and granite slabs just below Azurite Pass (6,700 ft) — roughly 3-3.5 hours from Horse Heaven Camp. From the pass, leave the trail and work northeast/east up a mix of krummholz, sand, scree, and talus to a broad shoulder around 7,400 ft, then follow a gently rising, ducked/cairned traverse across a series of ribs, gullies, and sandy slopes toward the base of the summit tower. The final push climbs a prominent south/southwest-facing gully — loose underfoot (watch for rockfall onto party members below) but no harder than Class 3 in dry conditions; it can hold firm snow well into summer, in which case an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) is worth carrying. Total one-way distance from the trailhead is on the order of 12-13 miles with about 6,700 ft of gain, so most parties backpack in to Horse Heaven Camp and climb from there rather than doing it car-to-car.
runs: traverse across a series of ribs gullies and sandy slopes

text: From Azurite Pass leave the trail and work northeast and east up krummholz, sand, scree and talus to a flat shoulder at about 7,400 ft — flat enough that parties cache overnight gear on it, and easy to relocate on the way down. Continue up the crest to roughly 7,600 ft, where a lower south summit obstructs the ridge and the well-cairned climbers' route drops off westward. From there a gently rising traverse crosses a series of ribs, gullies and sandy slopes, well marked with ducks and cairns, staying below the cliffs rather than in them, and crossing two or three short snow runnels that an ice axe handles. The traverse runs toward the peak's prominent west rib.
runs: a series of ribs gullies and sandy slopes well marked with ducks and cairns

text: Turn up too late and you meet the southwest face — that is the error to watch for. The correct gully is narrow at its base and cannot be seen from the ridge, so parties keep traversing hoping for something obvious, run out onto the imposing southwest face, and find it goes Class 4 in a hurry. The stated fix from those who have made that mistake is to retreat to the last gully to the south and go up that. The right line stays loose and never harder than short steps of Class 3 for roughly the last 200 ft to the top: if you are climbing more than short sections of Class 4, you are off route, and if you have drifted onto cleaner, more solid rock high on the gully's climber's-left wall you have left the gully floor for steeper and more exposed ground. One gully on this line pinches to about three feet, tight enough to touch both walls with your arms out — that constriction is a confirmation you are in a real line, not a warning.
runs: to the last gully to the south and

text: Follow the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail #611 through forest to the Anderson Butte Trail junction and stay left. Continue to the next junction, where the right fork drops to Lower Anderson Lake; bear left and climb to the saddle where the trail enters the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness.
runs: saddle where the trail enters the noisy diobsud wilderness

text: The standard descent reverses the ascent line: down the summit snow slopes and col, back onto and down the Diobsud Creek Glacier (roped, same crevasse caution as the approach), down through the steep loose gully/south-ridge terrain to Diobsud Lakes, then back over the Mt. Watson sidehill, saddle, and Anderson Lakes ridge path to the Watson Lakes Trailhead. This is a walk-off/glacier-descent — no rappels are used on the standard round trip; the technical difficulty is glacier travel and loose, steep downclimbing rather than anything requiring rope-anchored lowering. Parties continuing north as part of a longer Bacon-Hagan-Blum (or Watson-Bacon-Hagan-Blum) traverse instead descend from the summit down quick snow slopes to the "Bacon Tarns" (small glacial-melt ponds on a rock bench below the Green Lake Glacier), then follow heather and meadow along Bacon's north ridge, passing high above Green Lake toward Hidden Lake, continuing the traverse rather than returning to the Watson Lakes trailhead. Either way, expect the same loose-rock and brush hazards on the south-ridge gully in reverse, and re-assess glacier conditions/crevasse bridges on the return trip since afternoon snow softening changes the picture from the morning ascent.
runs: glacial melt ponds on a rock bench below the green lake glacier

text: Take the Watson Lakes Trail from the road end and, at the saddle beyond the Lower Anderson Lake fork, leave the maintained tread for a hiker's path running south along the ridge high above Lower Anderson Lake. The path opens into meadows and reaches Upper Anderson Lake — the last easy water. Leave the lake heading northeast up a short wooded gully and continue that way onto open moraine and heather slopes near 5,300 ft. Traverse under the Watson peaks and drop to about 5,000 ft to get around a buttress on their east side, then climb to a saddle at 5,360 ft and cross to the south side of the ridge. Continue east, losing a little height toward the next low point in the ridge, a saddle near 4,900 ft, crossing a short buttress on easy ledges on the way. A good camp sits at 5,900 ft, half a mile northeast of Bacon Peak.

text: Four vertical steps of roughly 300, 400, 220 and 250 ft, separated by spacious ledges, lead to the summit ridge. The second step is the crux, with 120-degree roof sections, delicate vertical climbing and protection poor enough that the first ascent resorted to aid and bolts; parties commonly bivy on the ledge above it. A few hundred feet of scrambling above the last step tops out. Do not plan on reversing the wall — the accepted way down is the non-technical walk-off on the far side of the mountain, and no fixed rappel stations should be assumed anywhere on the face.
runs: separated by spacious ledges lead to the summit

text: From US 2 at Baring, near milepost 41, turn north onto 635th Place NE, cross the railroad tracks, keep left at the junction, and continue onto Forest Road 6024 for about 4 miles to the Barclay Lake trailhead.
runs: north onto 635th place ne cross the railroad tracks

text: Thin ramp then stemming corner with knobs to a testy balance crux high up; 3 bolts plus small gear for crux.
runs: stemming corner with knobs to a testy balance crux

text: Traverse loose south-facing slopes below Points 6592 and 6822, crossing a rock rib, to this saddle on Bear's NW ridge — the standard bivy for the North Buttress, roughly 21 miles and two days from the trailhead.
runs: points 6592 and 6822 crossing a rock rib to

text: True summit horn gained via seven pitches of 5.10 climbing up the buttress above the couloir; descend west on the south side of the crest, then downclimb a short 3rd-class gully back toward the saddle camp.
runs: west on the south side of the crest

text: Blocky climbing to the top of the buttress, from where it's a scramble to the true summit.
runs: blocky climbing to the top of the buttress from

text: Follow the Chilliwack River Trail about 5 more miles down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence (the camp there is closed). Ford Bear Creek and climb steep, brushy timber and then huckleberry and slide alder east to the meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse below Points 6592 and 6822, crossing a rock rib, to the saddle camp at 6,480'. The long off-trail climb makes this the hardest approach day.

text: Starts on a shallow rib at the lowest point of the slab, with beautiful clean, solid, grippy low-angle stone and minimal breaks. After roughly 2,000+ ft of fun, sustained 4th-class climbing the line naturally angles right and joins Timeless Treasure for brief, unexposed low-5th moves up overlaps trending up and right to the SE shoulder; easy scrambling leads to the summit block, though rock quality noticeably deteriorates on the final three pitches.
runs: brief unexposed low 5th moves up overlaps trending up and right to the se shoulder easy scrambling leads

text: Begins at the lowest part of the slab on a shallow rib; clean, solid, grippy low-angle stone; after roughly 2,000+ ft naturally angles right to join Timeless Treasure.
